members.name: chevronPlacement
members.description:
Where the open indicator sits, or whether there is one.

`auto` resolves to `end`, which is where a reader scanning a list of
summaries expects it: the label starts at the same x on every row, and the
indicator is found once at the edge rather than shifting with the text.
`start` is for a tree-like reading, where the indicator leads the label.
`none` is for a row that carries its own affordance and would otherwise
have two.

declarations.description:

`footer`. An omitted region takes no space, so a card with only content needs
no wrapper markup at all.

`media` runs edge to edge and clips to the card's corners, so an image needs
no inset correction. Set `orientation="horizontal"` to move it alongside the
header, content, and footer stack rather than above it.

Regions are bare slots with no wrapper element, so an omitted one occupies no
space without the card having to detect that it is missing. Style slotted
content directly rather than reaching for a part: a header is whatever
element you slotted, not a wrapper we put around it.

declarations.description:
The host is the flex container itself and the only child is a slot, so the
element adds no box of its own: `<helix-flex>` costs exactly the `<div>` it
replaces.

There is no separate Stack. A stack is this with `direction="column"`, and a
second element whose whole definition is one default of the first is a name
to learn rather than a capability to gain.

Gap takes a space token name rather than a length, so spacing stays on the
scale. A layout that can say `gap="13px"` is one that will.

Presentation only, so there is no headless tier: the split exists to keep
behavior separate from styling, and this is entirely styling.

members.name: applyTemplate
members.description:
Writes the track list into the shadow root's own stylesheet.

Into a `<style>` rather than onto `this.style`, and the difference is
hydration. An inline style on the host is an attribute the element gives
itself once it upgrades, so a React consumer's server markup does not have
it and hydration reports a mismatch it will not patch up. The shadow root
is not part of the tree React hydrates, so a rule written there is free.

The element is filled imperatively because Lit refuses expressions inside
`<style>`: it is an invalid binding location and throws while rendering
rather than at build time. Hence a static, empty element in the template
and its `textContent` set here.

It sets a custom property rather than the track list itself. A shadow
root's adopted stylesheets cascade *after* its own `<style>` elements, and
`static styles` is adopted, so a `grid-template-columns` here lost to the
one in the stylesheet and every `min` grid came out a single column. The
stylesheet only ever reads `--_grid-template`, so there is nothing to
lose against.

The consequence is that a server-rendered grid falls back to the
stylesheet's single column until it upgrades. That is why `columns` is also
expressed as plain CSS below: the fixed-count case, which can be enumerated,
needs no JavaScript at all, and only `min` depends on this.

declarations.description:
Two properties, and they answer different questions. `as` is the element, which decides the document outline and what a screen reader announces. `appearance` is the treatment, which decides size, weight, leading, and tracking together. They are separate because they genuinely come apart: a section's second heading sometimes has to look smaller without lying about the outline, and a `

` sometimes has to read as a caption. They default to matching, so the common case is `as="h2"` and nothing else. The pairing is resolved in CSS rather than by computing an attribute, so the element writes nothing to its own host: `as="h2"` picks up the heading ramp through a selector, and setting `appearance` takes the pairing rule out of play. Deriving it in `willUpdate` worked, but it put an attribute on the host that the server's markup did not have, which is a hydration mismatch in every React consumer. **Size, weight, and leading are not properties.** Exposing them separately offers a few hundred combinations of which a handful are right, and every caller then picks one. An appearance is a decision the system already made: the ramp is named, and a page built from it is consistent because there was nothing else to choose. `tone` stays separate, because colour carries state rather than typography. Folding it in would mean `caption-danger` and `label-primary` and the rest of the cross product, which is the explosion `appearance` exists to prevent.
declarations.name: HelixText

declarations.description:
The indicator travels between items rather than the fill swapping. A fill
that appears on one item as it disappears from another is two changes at once
and reads as a flicker; one object moving is something the eye follows, and
it says where the selection came from as well as where it went.

It animates `translate` and `inline-size`. Width is a layout property and the
rule is transform and opacity only, but the indicator is out of flow, so
animating its width reflows nothing else. Scaling instead would distort the
corner radius, which is worse than the exception.

members.description: Items a reader can actually reach: not inside a collapsed branch.

members.name: syncItems
members.description:
Pushes tree-owned state down: which item is selected, which holds the tab
stop, and how deep each one sits.

Depth is computed here rather than by each item counting its own ancestors,
so an item moved in the tree gets the right indent without knowing it moved.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

Every component that is a landmark, a list item, or a cell used to write
`role` onto its own host in `willUpdate`. That is an attribute the element
adds to itself after it upgrades, so a React consumer's server markup never
has it and hydration reports a mismatch on every one of them.
`ElementInternals` exists for exactly this: it sets the implicit role an
author's `role` attribute still overrides, and it writes nothing.

Available during server rendering: Lit's shim implements
`attachInternals`, verified, so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

events.description: Fired when an item is chosen. Dispatched by the item and listened for here, because the tree is what a consumer holds a reference to.

declarations.description:
No chrome of its own: a toolbar is a place controls sit, and a border around
them would be a second frame inside whatever already frames the bar.
declarations.name: HelixToolbar

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the toolbar.

members.name: orientation
members.description: Which way the arrow keys move.

members.name: controls
members.description:
Focusable controls, in document order.

Asks each child for its own focus target rather than matching tag names, so
a toolbar holds anything, including elements this package has never heard
of. Client only: there is no tree to walk on the server.

members.name: setTabStop
members.description:
Moves the single tab stop to one control.

Prefers the control's own `focusable` property to writing `tabindex` on it.
The attribute is a change to markup the consumer rendered, which a React
consumer's hydration reports and does not patch up; a control that offers
the property moves the stop inside its own shadow root instead.

`tabindex` stays as the fallback, because a toolbar has to hold controls
this package has never heard of.

members.name: claimTabStop
members.description:
Sets the first tab stop once every custom control has upgraded.

A custom element has no properties at all before it upgrades, so a pass
that ran first would find no `focusable`, take the `tabindex` fallback, and
write the very attribute this exists to avoid.

members.name: axis
members.description:
The orientation in force.

Unset is horizontal, and stays unset: the default is the absent attribute,
so a reflected default cannot appear on the host after hydration.

declarations.description:
Indent comes from the `level` the tree sets, as a multiple of one hook, so a
node moved to another depth re-indents without any nested selector. Nesting
selectors by depth is the usual approach and stops working at whatever depth
nobody wrote a rule for.

The twisty rotates rather than swapping glyphs, so opening a branch is a
short movement instead of a substitution. Motion carries the state change;
the row itself stays flat.

members.description: Whether this item is the current one.

members.name: expanded
members.description: Whether a branch is showing its children.

members.name: level
members.description:
Depth from the root, set by the tree so indentation needs no CSS nesting.

Not reflected. The tree assigns this after it upgrades, so an attribute
here would be a change to markup the consumer rendered and hydration would
report it. The indent it drives is written onto the row instead, inside the
shadow root, which is not part of the tree React hydrates.
